text: I will discreetly touch her brow with the oil of olive, trace the sign of the palms, and whisper 'be at peace' with the words of the balsam.

I traced the sign gently, the oil's warmth soothing, as I whispered the words. My touch, a balm on the fevered brow, a whisper of hope in the ancient forest. It is done, and in this place, my actions held their own sacred weight.

I will breathe in the smell of the hay stack, wipe the blade, oil it, look along the edge for nicks and take them out on the stone. Check every rivet on the mail and restitch the strap before it breaks.
I will take up my blade and oil it, then check every rivet on the mail, for one gone and the rings start to open.
I will pull the rope, catch the sally, and strike the bell for the feast to celebrate the harvest, or for the death of a lord, or to sound the alarm for a raid.

I completed the track to the storage shed. My success allowed me to learn trailcraft. For the dead, I know the knell and its meaning - feast or death. The strike of the bell rings out, a solemn alarm.
I notice the polished leg-holes, but there's no ripe one to be had. Quick as I can, I'll move on to the next bush, lest I waste more time.
I will gently touch her hand, introducing myself with a smile, as the ripe berries come away easily and the basket fills faster than expected.
I notice an oak tree by the byre. Its spreading crown with deep fissured bark and heavy boughs stands in stark contrast to the neglect around me.

I see the blacksmith working, her hands moving with practiced ease, sparks dancing as she strikes the anvil. Her eyes hold a weariness, a silent acknowledgment of the day's work not yet accounted for.
I will breathe in the smell of the hay stack, and if it is sweet and clean as it should be, I will know our animals have been fed well.
I will slowly dip the wick into the slow-smelling, well-rendered fat, let it cool and set, then introduce myself discreetly to her, watching the steady flame grow.
I will breathe in the scent of the hay stack, signing my name and holding the deed for the barn, naming it and holding it, with two witnesses, and affixing the proper seal on the right ribbon.

I managed to follow the courtyard-storage shed track. It felt like a successful journey, leading to the storage shed. There, I learned trailcraft. Now, I must draw up the deeds - the formula, signature, and seal - to make this official.
I mastered trailcraft, and in its cold relish, I found a cold comfort, relishing the dominance over the weak as a farmer might over his livestock.
"Abigail, see this. A stone bench, worn smooth in the center by time. What do you think it means?"

I notice the weathered oak stocks beside the cross, their leg-holes polished by use. The sight draws me to hidden meanings, as the second message lies in the polish's pattern and the very essence of the wooden objects, keys to a forgotten ritual.
I observe the central stone-rimmed well at the square's heart, a wooden bucket on its rope. To listen to it, I'll rely on the plain ways of country folk, hidden meanings in every stone and rope.
I will breathe in the smell of the hay stack as I drive the nail through the white line of the hot shoe fitted to the wall hoof.

I set the shoe to this hoof, hot from the anvil, fitting it tight. With each nail driven, I felt the sole and wall, avoiding the frog. The task done, the creature's secrets learned, I stood back to admire the fit, a success that felt like magic in this forest.
I laid the shaft upon the moss, straightened it with care, and sighted down again. The feathers twist as they should, snugly bound and true. A snail's lore learned, thanks to this close scrutiny.
I adjusted the shaft, straightened the feathers with a twist, and fitted the head. Now I know the trail, thanks to this success.
I spy a laden branch, ripe fruit nestled among the full basket, my contented eye marks the oak's spreading crown with deep-fissured bark and heavy boughs.

I notice a laden branch by the cross, ripe stocks ready to pick, but there's nothing worth gathering here. I'll turn my eye to the next ripe fruit on the branch and fill my basket with the best growth.
I will gently chip away at the rind, revealing the marrow within, introducing myself steadily and respectfully.
I cracked through the rind, found the marrow inside, and learned the trail. Satisfied, I ground away, the good part waiting inside.
I will align the green bark layers by eye, make a clean cut long and at the same angle on both, then bind them tight as a join, not too tight to strangle.
I lined up the snail's shell with the bark's green layer, matched them precisely as if joining two trees. My work was done, the snail's lore I had learned, and now it binds tightly, the join secure.
I learned trailcraft. It fills me with warmth seen from outside - the window, the smoke, the smell of a meal that is not mine, and makes me feel settled, no longer in a hurry.
I felt warmth from the window smoke, the smell of a meal not mine, and it made me glad and lighter than before.
I cackle at the sound of a laid egg, under the oak. It's a broody's growl, and I find the hidden nest by the deep-fissured bark, heavy boughs.
I found the hidden nest, heard the cackle - an egg out of place. The broody's growl echoed, she'd laid again. Thanks to this, I learned creature lore, my hands kneaded the earth.
I note the oak's spreading crown, its deep-ridged bark and sturdy branches, and let its honesty calm my heart.
I notice the blacksmith of the village, a woman. Her ears are alert, her eye watches the anvil, her tail clamped, and her breath steady. A wry smile hints at her mind, calculating and sharp.

I will shift my weight onto the horse's back, feeling the back stiffen before it answers with a shy, and the ears flicker as I speak gently, 'easy,' 'what have you seen?' - you know the way better than I do.

I shifted my weight, the horse's back answering the command. Ears flicked, the creature's shyness before it happened. Success felt in the quiet of the forest, a close examination of the snail achieved.
I perceive the oak, its leaves laid with a breath, the vine entwined, all in gold and colour, a tiny world within the vastness of this ancient tree.

I followed the courtyard-track to the storage shed, my hands moving with a breath, smoothing and laying gold leaf as if it were a miniature work of art in a medieval monastery. The tiny figures and vines seemed to come to life, and I felt a sense of trailcraft and achievement, like a saint in the hollow of the letter.

I will drop the resin-coated grains onto the glowing coal, creating a sweet smoke that swirls upwards. I will then discreetly approach her, my scent mingling with that of frankincense, my swing indicating the direction of our conversation.

I have followed the track to the storage shed, smoke rising from my incense swings. This rite is done, and I've learned trailcraft. The resin sends its smoke where it's needed, meaning clear and strong.
I will gently approach her, introducing myself under the scent of olive and balsam, as a sign of peace.
I completed my task, touching the snail with the oil of knowledge. Its lore is whispered through the leaves, a blessing from the earth.
I will breathe in the scent of the hay stack, checking every straw for any signs of decay before it fails to support the weight above.
I will approach her discreetly, introducing myself by the village well.
I will breathe in the scent of the hay stack, marking the time with each inhale, a solemn toll for those who have passed.
I marked the path, following the courtyard to the storage shed. The success of my trailcraft announces to all, and I know it calls for a knell, as the day's work has ended.

I glance at the weathered oak stocks by the cross, noting the polished leg-holes. But there's nothing here worth picking, so I'll move to another bush nearby and fill my basket quicker than it takes to think this thought.
I will lightly strike up a chat with her, introducing myself swiftly.
I note an oak here, well-maintained with deep fissures on its bark and ample branches, indicating proper care.

I see the blacksmith working, her hammering with each blow, sparks flying. Her gaze is distant, as if she's counting something unseen. Her stance is steady, though it's uncomfortable to watch, suggesting she's keeping track of time or a count.
I will breathe in the scent of the hay stack, patient and exact, content with slow work done in its proper order and not hurried.
I will slowly approach her, introducing myself with gentle words.
I will inhale the scent of the hay stack.
I have succeeded in following the courtyard-storage shed track. My efforts have led me to the storage shed, where I have learned the craft of trailfinding.

I learned trailcraft. It fills me with cold, unhurried satisfaction, noticing first the small, weak beast before me, relishing the clean logic of power that crushes those who cannot defend themselves.
"Abigail, gaze upon this. I observed a stone bench worn smooth by time, its center worn deep. What do you find in it?"

I trust the weathered set of oak stocks not for their practical use but for the stories they hold, hidden in their polished leg-holes. My intent is to delve into their history, shrouded in silence, rather than turn my attention to what is plainly here.

I trust not the plain sense, for it hides the central stone-rimmed well at the square's heart, a wooden bucket on its rope. I seek to listen, to decipher the hidden lore of the plain ways of country folk, as I must trust no modern truths in this medieval world.

I worked my will, close and steady, as the snail's shell held still beneath me. My task done, I felt a quiet satisfaction, knowing all there was to be learned.
I saw it clearly, its shell smooth and secret. This close inspection, though, did not bring joy.
I saw the courtyard track through the storage shed and straightened it to perfection. Success brings relief, but perfection is unattainable, and I must sight down my shaft once more.
I find an oak tree, spreading its broad crown with deep-fissured bark and heavy boughs, ripe for closer inspection.
I spot a set of oak stocks beside the cross, their leg-holes polished by use, but there's nothing ripe here. I'll turn my attention to the ripe produce in my garden instead.
I will softly call her name, then introduce myself, sharing a loaf of bread.
I completed the track, learned the storage shed's secrets. Worth the effort, inside is reward.
I will align the thin green layers of the scion and stock by eye, ensuring they meet precisely as they breathe in the hay stack smell.
I have matched the thin green layers precisely, my task completed. Now the snail lore is known, my work well done.
I learned trailcraft. It makes me feel settled, and no longer in a hurry. A wistful ache stays, seeing comfort others have.
I saw how they gathered, laughed, shared, and felt at ease, a lightness not mine, but wistful and aching to know.
I cackle at the sound, a spreading broad-crowned oak with deep-fissured bark and heavy boughs - it's where the nest lies hidden.
I found her, the snail in the crevice. Now, I must close the cover of the nest, gently.
I gaze upon an oak tree, its spreading crown with deep-fissured bark and heavy branches drawing my attention. Trusting these plain signs, I find peace and steadiness here.

I notice the blacksmith of the village, a woman. Her eyes hold a quiet worry that her work does not fully account for, and she stands watchful, as if counting something. Her calm trust in plain signs steadies me, and my attention is drawn to her ears first.
I will breathe in the scent of the hay stack, attending to the first small sign and answering calmly, never by force.
I examined it closely, the snail's shell a tiny world. This success taught me much, creature lore to learn.
I take a deep breath, my gaze drawn to the oak. Its spreading crown, deep-barked and laden with heavy branches, holds a world within its gnarled arms.

I succeeded in following the courtyard-storage shed track, my breath raised and smoothed the gold as I breathed on it. The hare in the margin chased a snail, and learning trailcraft felt like a page took weeks to complete, its colours ground from stone and earth, each stroke revealing a whole world in my hands.
I will walk to the village well, where the elders gather, and with hands clasped, I will discreetly strike up a conversation with her, introducing myself.
I made my way through the courtyard, following the track to the storage shed. My steps and every breath carried the scent of my labor, marking each step with purpose and reverence.
